content: Acetaminophen infusion is an analgesic and antipyretic medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of pain and fever. It is not a substitute for professional healthcare advice, and its use should align with FDA-approved guidelines. The educational content provided is based on FDA package inserts, the National Library of Medicine, and clinical guidelines. Black Box Warning Acetaminophen infusion carries a Black Box Warning due to the risk of hepatic injury, including liver failure and death, if the maximum recommended daily dose is exceeded. This includes all routes of administration (oral, intravenous, and rectal) and all acetaminophen-containing products. Patients should ensure that the total daily dose does not exceed 4000 mg for adults and adolescents weighing 50 kg or more. Indications and Dosage Adults and Adolescents (≥50 kg): The recommended dose is 1000 mg every 6 hours or 650 mg every 4 hours, with a maximum single dose of 1000 mg and a maximum daily dose of 4000 mg. Pediatric Patients (<50 kg): The dose is based on weight, with a maximum single dose of 15 mg/kg and a maximum daily dose of 75 mg/kg. Acetaminophen infusion can be administered as a single or repeated dose for acute pain or fever. No dose adjustment is required when switching between oral and intravenous forms in adults and adolescents weighing ≥50 kg. Administration Guidelines Administer acetaminophen infusion intravenously over 15 minutes using aseptic technique. Do not use the vial if particulate matter or discoloration is observed. For doses less than 1000 mg, withdraw the appropriate amount and transfer it to a separate container before administration. Pediatric doses up to 60 mL should be administered using a syringe pump over 15 minutes. Monitor the end of the infusion to prevent air embolism, especially if acetaminophen infusion is the primary infusion. Contraindications Known hypersensitivity to acetaminophen or any excipients in the intravenous formulation. Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease. Warnings Hepatic Injury: Exceeding the recommended dose may result in severe liver damage. Patients should be informed of the risks and advised to discontinue use if signs of hypersensitivity or skin reactions occur. Serious Skin Reactions: Rare but potentially fatal skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), have been reported. Patients should discontinue use at the first sign of rash or hypersensitivity. Hypersensitivity and Anaphylaxis: Post-marketing reports include cases of anaphylaxis requiring emergency medical attention. Symptoms include facial swelling, respiratory distress, and rash. Discontinue use immediately if allergic symptoms occur. Adverse Reactions Common adverse reactions in adults include nausea, vomiting, headache, and insomnia. In pediatric patients, common reactions include nausea, vomiting, constipation, pruritus, agitation, and atelectasis. Rare adverse events include anemia, tachycardia, injection site pain, hepatic enzyme elevation, and pulmonary edema. Overdose Acute overdose can cause potentially fatal hepatic necrosis, renal tubular necrosis, hypoglycemic coma, and thrombocytopenia. Early symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and malaise, with hepatic toxicity becoming apparent 48-72 hours post-ingestion. Treatment involves obtaining a serum acetaminophen level and administering N-acetylcysteine (NAC) as an antidote. Liver function tests should be monitored. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Acetaminophen infusion should only be used if clearly needed. Epidemiological data on oral acetaminophen use during pregnancy show no increased risk of major congenital malformations. Nursing Mothers: Acetaminophen is excreted in breast milk in small amounts. Caution is advised when administering to nursing women. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy are supported for patients aged 2 years and older. Effectiveness in children under 2 years has not been established. Geriatric Use: No significant differences in safety or efficacy were observed in elderly patients compared to younger adults, but greater sensitivity in some older individuals cannot be ruled out. Renal Impairment: In severe renal impairment, longer dosing intervals and reduced total daily doses may be necessary. Hepatic Impairment: Acetaminophen is contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment and should be used cautiously in patients with liver disease. Pharmacology The precise mechanism of action is not fully understood but is thought to involve central actions. Acetaminophen is metabolized in the liver via glucuronidation, sulfation, and oxidation pathways. The reactive metabolite NAPQI is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione. Less than 5% of the drug is excreted unchanged in the urine, with more than 90% excreted within 24 hours. Clinical Studies Clinical trials have demonstrated the efficacy of acetaminophen infusion in reducing pain intensity and fever in adults and pediatric patients. It has been shown to reduce opioid consumption in postoperative pain management, although the clinical benefit of this reduction was not demonstrated. Nonclinical Toxicology Long-term studies in animals have shown no evidence of carcinogenicity at doses up to 8 times the maximum human daily dose. However, high doses may impair fertility and cause fetal toxicity in animal studies. How Supplied Acetaminophen infusion is supplied in 100 mL glass vials containing 1000 mg of acetaminophen (10 mg/mL). It is intended for single use, and any unused portion must be discarded.
